content: Serious adverse events (AEs) that led to the permanent discontinuation of a medication are documented in detail within the EndTB dataset, using the MSF severity scale. Definitions for these events are provided at the end of the document. However, this information is inconsistently available across datasets (~8000 patients in 30 datasets) and is defined as grade 3–5 or serious AEs that resulted in permanent discontinuation of the medication. These events may have been differentially ascertained in the IPD 2019 dataset, potentially confounding comparisons of AE rates, especially for drugs used more or less frequently in the two datasets. If permission is granted by all parties, we will compare AEs in the EndTB dataset with those detected in the NixTB study. These two studies had comparable AE detection intensities, although they used different definitions and methods for AE assessment. Adherence, measured as the percentage of doses taken or other metrics, is available in the EndTB dataset but not in the IPD 2019 dataset. Therefore, adherence will only be described for the EndTB dataset. The IPD 2019 dataset was assembled in 2018 and includes 53 datasets from 40 countries/regions, containing records for 13,000 patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). This dataset builds upon the IPD 2018 dataset, which was analyzed to address PICO questions developed by the WHO MDR-TB guidelines development group (GdG). The IPD 2018 dataset itself was based on an earlier dataset assembled in 2016–2017 to address questions from the CDC/ATS/IDSA/ERS GdG. While the analyses informing the CDC/ATS/IDSA/ERS guidelines were published in The Lancet in September 2018, the guidelines themselves have not yet been published. The IPD 2019 dataset represents an update of the IPD 2018 dataset. We anticipate adding data from one national surveillance program in South Africa. To avoid duplication, we will remove previous records of patients treated in the EndTB observational study that were included in the IPD 2018 dataset. Additionally, we may incorporate two other datasets submitted in response to a public call for data contributions. The EndTB dataset includes 1094 patients with MDR-TB treated with bedaquilineand/or delamanid-containing regimens between April 1, 2015, and March 31, 2017, as part of an observational study conducted by three NGOs: Partners in Health (PIH), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), and Interactive Research and Development (IRD). The question of the optimal duration of bedaquiline (BDQ) therapy is challenging due to several potential sources of bias in observational studies. For example, patients who survive longer on rifampin-resistant TB (RR-TB) treatment may receive longer courses of bedaquiline, leading to an overestimation of the benefits of prolonged treatment. This is known as immortal time bias. Additionally, the decision to prolong bedaquiline therapy may vary based on patient factors, country, and time. For instance, patients with poor initial treatment responses, weak regimens without bedaquiline, or limited treatment options due to resistance profiles or treatment-emergent toxicities may be more likely to receive prolonged bedaquiline. Simply comparing outcomes between those who received prolonged bedaquiline and those who did not could underestimate the benefits of prolonged therapy due to time-varying confounding by indication. In the EndTB study, the use of prolonged bedaquiline varied across countries and over time. Some countries extended bedaquiline use for nearly all patients, while others did not permit its extension due to national guidelines. At other sites, clinicians became more comfortable with the drug over time, leading to increased use of prolonged therapy. Similar issues arise with other drugs, such as linezolid, where patients may receive longer treatment if they do not experience treatment-limiting toxicity (~1 in 5 patients for linezolid). While our proposed analysis approach aims to minimize many sources of bias, it may not be possible to eliminate all biases. The precise duration of bedaquiline therapy can be defined in the EndTB dataset to the exact number of days, but real-world factors such as missed visits, clinic cancellations, holidays, or bad weather can introduce variability of up to a month. To address this, we will first define a frequency distribution of bedaquiline duration to identify optimal cut-points for each duration. For example, based on recent analyses, a 6-month duration might include patients treated for 150–200 days. In this statistical analysis plan (SAP), references to durations such as 24 weeks, 36 weeks, or 52 weeks will include a range of weeks determined from the initial descriptive analysis. Comparing results between the EndTB and IPD 2019 datasets presents challenges due to differences in patient populations, treatments, and other factors. The EndTB study was conducted by agencies and centers with different patient populations, resources, and clinical expertise compared to those in the IPD 2019 dataset. The IPD 2019 dataset includes data from a broader variety of settings, including national MDR surveillance systems, which may result in different outcomes due to unmeasured confounding. Mixed models will be used to account for heterogeneity between datasets. There is a perception that EndTB sites treated more complex patients with comorbidities and other challenges (e.g., homelessness, history of incarceration, IV drug use, alcohol use), making it more difficult to develop effective regimens. Additionally, the extent and quality of data, particularly on-treatment longitudinal observations and follow-up for recurrent disease, as well as methods for safety data collection and reporting, may differ between datasets. In the EndTB dataset, all patients received delamanid (DLM), bedaquiline, or both, whereas many patients in the IPD dataset received neither. If delamanid is highly effective, this could substantially affect comparisons of the no-bedaquiline group in the IPD 2019 cohort versus the EndTB dataset, as all EndTB patients received delamanid. Therefore, exposure to delamanid will be controlled for in all analyses. The diversity of settings and patients in the IPD 2019 dataset provides an excellent opportunity to compare treatment-related covariates across different contexts, potentially leading to more generalizable findings. The results from Questions 1 and 2 will assess whether the effect of bedaquiline use beyond six months is similar in the EndTB and IPD datasets after accounting for numerous confounders. Any confounding effect of delamanid will be managed by controlling for its use in all analyses. The analysis for Question 3 will evaluate the benefit of bedaquiline for six months versus longer durations versus no bedaquiline, adjusting for delamanid use, data source, and other covariates. The reference group for this analysis will be patients who received bedaquiline for six months. While the IPD 2019 dataset has limitations compared to the EndTB dataset, it offers important advantages for analyzing bedaquiline duration, including greater diversity of settings and patients, which enhances the generalizability of results. This diversity also increases the likelihood of capturing a broader range of patients receiving longer bedaquiline durations, potentially reducing unmeasured confounding. Finally, the larger number of patients treated with specific regimens or durations of bedaquiline increases statistical power. To define time cut-offs for bedaquiline use, we will examine the frequency distribution of bedaquiline duration to identify inter-modal cut-points that best discriminate between patients treated for 24 weeks, 36 weeks, or 52 weeks. Patients who died or were lost to follow-up will be excluded from this analysis to ensure the population assessed includes only those who could have received the drug to the specified time point. This approach will also be applied to the sensitivity analysis population. Recognizing that any selected time point will dichotomize some patients with only slight differences in treatment duration, selecting inter-modal points should minimize this issue. Descriptive analyses will characterize subgroups of patients who did not receive bedaquiline, those who received it for at least one month but less than six months, and those who received it for at least 24 weeks, further subdivided into 24–36 weeks and >36 weeks. These analyses will include site of treatment, baseline/pre-treatment characteristics (e.g., sex, age, HIV status, comorbidities, prior TB treatment, AFB smear, CXR results, DST results, year of treatment initiation, and number of likely effective drugs used initially). The total number of drugs a patient is resistant to will also be considered, as greater resistance limits treatment options and increases the likelihood of bedaquiline extension. Statistical analyses will adjust for this covariate. We will also explore the use of delamanid descriptively, examining characteristics of patients who received delamanid alone, delamanid and bedaquiline, or bedaquiline alone. We will assess whether delamanid was used from the start or introduced later, as many patients received delamanid after several months of therapy. This raises the possibility of indication bias (e.g., patients with poor initial responses) and immortal time bias (e.g., patients surviving longer to receive delamanid later). Median time to delamanid initiation and its distribution across sites will be described, as site-specific policies may influence its use.
